newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition gets Rome support, urges big crowds.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition gets Rome support, urges big crowds.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders, back from a one-day trip to Italy, said on Friday that Rome supported their battle over annulled elections but more people must turn out to back their cause.

"Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and all of Italy are sending their full support for our two-month-old struggle to have our November 17 election results recognised," Vuk Draskovic, one of the Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders, told about 15,000 to 20,000 demonstrators in Belgrade.
It was the 61st day of protests across Serbia against the government's decision to annul opposition victories in 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities for "irregularities".
With numbers of demonstrators down sharply, the opposition leaders said it was time for another big rally to try to approach the half million who turned out on Orthodox New Year.

"Tomorrow we must stage a mass protest to mark these two months and face the police in our own uniforms --- army reserve, civil defence, doctors, stewardesses, every possible uniform," Draskovic said.
"Uniforms will face uniforms tomorrow and we will mix with each other. Serbia is the one and only homeland of all of us -- both us and the police," he said.
During the two months of deadlock President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialist party has opposed every legal attempt to award the election victories to Zajedno.
On Thursday the Socialists appealed against an opposition victory in Serbia's second city Nis. The appeal was rejected on Friday, an opposition leader said.
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno co-leader, said the trip to Italy by Draskovic, Vesna Pesic and himself had not been intended to achieve a breakthrough.
Djindjic, who is due to meet German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel in Bonn on Sunday, said the trip to Rome had been purely a protocol visit.
"No mediation took place and none had been expected, as our position is clear. We are demanding the full implementation of the OSCE mission and we cannot back down from this."
"If someone needs persuading, it is Milosevic," Djindjic said, adding that Dini had said recognition of the November 17 results was a condition for "any further contacts with Milosevic and Belgrade".

The OSCE (Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe) sent a fact-finding mission to Serbia in December which found the elections had been fair. It backed this up on Thursday by saying Milosevic should reinstate the elections and stop doing so "piecemeal".

Draskovic said one of the subjects discussed in Rome had been the future of the Serbian province of Kosovo, where a Serb minority lives alongside an Albanian majority, among whom are shadowy militants who want the province to secede from Serbia.

"We said openly that this democratic movement for a new European, prosperous, democratic and powerful Serbia has struck terror into the hearts of Albanian political extremists of Kosovo," Draskovic said.
"They know that this democratic Serbia will mean the death knell of any dreams for some sort of independent Kosovo and its secession from Serbia," he added.

Draskovic said the Zajedno leaders would resolve the Kosovo problem by guaranteeing the human and ethnic rights of the province's Albanians, but that this could not be at the expense of "a lack of rights and the misfortune of our own people".
